nodes.summary: VOR stations broadcast 360 radials you can track like spokes of a wheel; the cockpit needle shows deviation from your chosen radial. NDBs are their simpler, older cousins — a beacon your needle simply points at.
nodes.deep_dive:
Before GPS, the sky was organized around VORs — VHF Omnidirectional Ranges. Each station broadcasts so that a receiver can tell which of 360° radials (magnetic courses FROM the station) it sits on. On the chart, each VOR wears a compass rose; in the cockpit, you tune its frequency (108.0–117.95 MHz), identify it by Morse code, and twist the OBS knob to choose a course.

The display (CDI) is elegantly simple: a vertical needle swings left or right showing whether the chosen course is left or right of you, full deflection meaning 10° or more off. A TO/FROM flag resolves ambiguity: with 360 selected and a TO flag, flying 360 takes you to the station. Center the needle, keep it centered with small corrections, and you are riding a radio beam. Twist, tune, identify — then track.

Key mental model: the VOR needle does not care which way your nose points. It only reports where you are relative to the chosen radial. That trips up every student once.

NDBs (non-directional beacons) are AM transmitters in the 190–535 kHz band; the cockpit ADF needle just points at the station like a compass to a magnet. Simple, but no course guidance — wind drift curves your path unless you compute corrections. NDBs are nearly extinct in the U.S., yet survive worldwide and in exam questions.

Distance comes from DME or GPS; two VOR radials crossed on a chart also fix your position — the classic triangulation.
nodes.advanced:
Instrument-rating preview and gotchas. VOR service volumes matter: a low VOR guarantees 40 NM at ~1,000–18,000 ft (terminal VORs less); beyond that, signals are unreliable — line of sight, like all VHF. Accuracy checks are a real regulation (91.171, for IFR): ±4° on a ground checkpoint, ±6° airborne, or ±4° between dual receivers. Reverse sensing — the needle working backwards because you selected the reciprocal course — is the classic trap; modern HSIs make it nearly impossible, round-dial CDIs make it a rite of passage.

The cone of confusion over the station flickers flags and swings needles — hold heading and wait. Radials are magnetic as of the station's last alignment; some old VORs are misaligned from today's variation by several degrees. The U.S. is retiring VORs down to a Minimum Operational Network (~590 stations) as a GPS backup, which is exactly why examiners still test VOR skills: when GPS jamming NOTAMs appear (they do, weekly), the twist-tune-identify pilot shrugs. Bearing TO an NDB: magnetic bearing = magnetic heading + relative bearing (MH + RB = MB), the one formula ADF questions ever need.

jargon_terms.definition: One of 360 magnetic courses radiating FROM a VOR station, like spokes from a hub.
Omni Bearing Selector — the knob that dials the course you want the VOR needle to reference.
Course Deviation Indicator — the needle showing how far left or right you are of the selected course.
Distance Measuring Equipment — paired with many VORs, giving slant-range distance to the station in NM.
Automatic Direction Finder — the receiver whose needle points directly at a tuned NDB.

nodes.title: GPS & Satellite Navigation
nodes.summary: GPS receivers triangulate position from satellite timing signals, giving position, groundspeed, and track anywhere on earth. It has revolutionized navigation — and created a new failure mode: blind trust.
nodes.deep_dive:
The Global Positioning System is a constellation of about 31 satellites, each broadcasting an exquisitely-timed signal. Your receiver measures how long each signal took to arrive, converts time to distance, and intersects those distances: four satellites yield latitude, longitude, altitude, and a time fix. No ground stations, no line-of-sight-to-a-VOR limits, works identically over Kansas and the Pacific.

What the panel GPS (or tablet) does with it: moving map with your airplane on the sectional, direct-to navigation to any airport or fix, groundspeed and track read directly (no computing winds), distance and time-to-destination continuously updated, and terrain/obstacle warnings. For VFR flying it is a situational-awareness miracle.

Aviation adds integrity layers consumer devices skip. RAIM — receiver autonomous integrity monitoring — cross-checks extra satellites to detect a lying signal. WAAS — the Wide Area Augmentation System — broadcasts corrections via geostationary satellites, tightening accuracy to about 1–2 meters and enabling precision-like instrument approaches.

The cautionary tale every instructor tells: the magenta-line pilot who follows the GPS course into airspace, terrain, or fuel exhaustion because the box said 'direct'. GPS answers 'where am I?' perfectly; it does not answer 'is this a good idea?'
- Best practice: navigate by pilotage and dead reckoning, confirm with GPS — not the reverse — until the habits are set.
nodes.advanced:
The deeper stack. GPS satellites orbit at ~10,900 NM (MEO), each carrying atomic clocks; your fix's weak axis is vertical, so GPS altitude can differ from barometric by tens of feet legitimately (and GPS altitude is geometric — never substitute it for the altimeter). Handhelds and tablets are legal ONLY as situational awareness for VFR: certified IFR navigation requires a TSO'd installed receiver with current database. Database currency runs on the same 28-day AIRAC cycle the whole world's nav data uses.

Threats are real and current: GPS jamming NOTAMs cover wide areas during military exercises, and spoofing has become a live issue near conflict zones. Mitigation is layered: RAIM prediction before IFR flights, WAAS integrity, the retained VOR Minimum Operational Network, and — for you — chart-and-clock skills that never lose satellite lock. GNSS is the umbrella term: GPS (US), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU), BeiDou (China); many modern receivers listen to several. And ADS-B, the surveillance system replacing radar, is GPS-derived: your position broadcast is only as honest as your GPS — one more reason integrity monitoring is not optional plumbing.

jargon_terms.definition: Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring — the GPS receiver's self-check that detects a faulty satellite signal.
Wide Area Augmentation System — satellite-broadcast corrections improving GPS accuracy to ~1–2 m for aviation.
The GPS function that draws a straight magenta course from present position to any waypoint.
The worldwide 28-day schedule on which navigation databases and charts are updated.

nodes.title: Right-of-Way Rules
nodes.summary: When aircraft converge, fixed rules decide who yields: distress trumps everything, the less-maneuverable aircraft has priority, head-on traffic breaks right, and the lower aircraft on final owns the runway.
nodes.deep_dive:
The sky's traffic law lives in 14 CFR 91.113, and it starts with a sentence that overrides the rest: regardless of who has the right of way, every pilot must see and avoid. Winning the rules argument in an accident report is not winning.

The hierarchy, most-privileged first: aircraft in distress; then balloons; gliders; aircraft towing or refueling others; airships; and finally powered airplanes and helicopters, at the bottom of the pecking order. The logic is pure maneuverability — a balloon cannot yield to you, so you yield to it.

Geometry rules for same-category encounters:
- Converging: the aircraft on the RIGHT has the right of way (like cars at a stop sign). The other pilot gives way — and never crosses over, under, or ahead unless well clear.
- Head-on: both aircraft alter course to the RIGHT. Nobody has priority; both act.
- Overtaking: the aircraft being overtaken has the right of way; the faster aircraft passes WELL clear to the RIGHT.

Landing: an aircraft on final approach, or actually landing, has right of way over aircraft on the ground or in the air. Between two aircraft approaching to land, the LOWER one has priority — but the rule explicitly forbids abusing this by diving in front of, or cutting off, another aircraft on final.

Memory hooks: 'right is right' covers converging, head-on, and overtaking; 'low bird lands first' covers the pattern.
nodes.advanced:
The layers exams love. 91.113 gives an aircraft in distress right of way over ALL other air traffic — and 91.3 lets that pilot break any rule to the extent required. On converging courses of DIFFERENT categories, category beats geometry: a glider converging from your left still has priority over your airplane. Water operations get their own section (91.115), same right-is-right logic plus keep-clear obligations for vessels.

On the surface, ATC instructions supersede the framework at towered fields; at non-towered fields the landing hierarchy plus common courtesy govern, and AC 90-66C explicitly discourages using the low-aircraft rule to leapfrog a stabilized pattern. Also connected: minimum safe altitudes (91.119) — 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft horizontally over congested areas, 500 ft above the surface elsewhere, and 'no closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure' in open areas; and formation flight requires prior arrangement between all pilots (91.111). Night ID trivia with a purpose: red navigation light on the LEFT wingtip, green on the RIGHT — see red on your right at your altitude, and the other aircraft has the right of way and is crossing left-to-right... treat red-right-returning as 'give way'.

jargon_terms.definition: Two aircraft on paths that will intersect — the one on the right has priority.
The last straight segment of the landing pattern, aligned with the runway.
The federal regulation defining right-of-way between aircraft in flight and when landing.
Broad aircraft classification (airplane, glider, balloon, airship...) used by the right-of-way hierarchy.

nodes.title: IMSAFE: The Pilot Preflight
nodes.summary: Airplanes get a preflight inspection; so must pilots. IMSAFE checks Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, and Emotion before every flight — because the most failure-prone component in aviation is human.
nodes.deep_dive:
Walk the checklist honestly before every flight:
- Illness — Am I sick? A head cold that is trivial at sea level can become disabling ear/sinus pain during descent, and congestion medicine brings its own problems.
- Medication — Am I taking anything that affects judgment or alertness? Many common antihistamines and sleep aids are explicitly disqualifying; the FAA publishes go/no-go lists, and 'wait 5 half-lives after the last dose' is the standing guidance.
- Stress — Job, money, family? Stress consumes the mental bandwidth that weather diversions and radio calls need. The insidious part: stressed pilots feel an urge to 'just get there'.
- Alcohol — The regulation (91.17) is 8 hours bottle-to-throttle AND under 0.04% blood alcohol AND no residual impairment. The safe personal rule is far more conservative: 24 hours, because hangover impairment at altitude is real.
- Fatigue — The sneakiest item, because fatigue's first casualty is your ability to notice you are fatigued. Studies put moderate sleep deprivation on par with legal intoxication.
- Emotion — Anger, grief, a fresh argument. Strong emotion narrows attention exactly the way alcohol does.

Any item failing the sniff test is a no-go — and unlike weather, nobody will see it on radar. Self-certification is the loneliest and most important go/no-go decision in flying.

IMSAFE is one member of a checklist family: PAVE frames the whole flight (Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures) — IMSAFE is the deep-dive on the P.
nodes.advanced:
The regulatory scaffolding under the mnemonic. 61.53 prohibits acting as a required crewmember while any known medical condition (or its treatment) would prevent meeting medical-certificate standards — it applies between medical exams, making YOU the continuous medical certifier. 91.17's alcohol rule has a fourth prong people forget: no carriage of an obviously intoxicated passenger. The 0.04% limit comes with a practical warning — metabolism averages ~0.015%/hour, so 'legal' after a heavy night is arithmetic fantasy.

On medication: the FAA's DO-NOT-ISSUE/DO-NOT-FLY lists and the 5-half-life rule (e.g., diphenhydramine/Benadryl: minimum 60 hours) are searchable on faa.gov; when in doubt, call an AME before flying, not after. Fatigue science: the FAA recognizes both acute and chronic fatigue plus circadian lows (2–6 a.m. and mid-afternoon); the airline world's fix — mandatory rest rules — has no GA equivalent, so your personal minimums must do that job. Finally, hazardous-attitude doctrine pairs with IMSAFE: anti-authority ('rules are for others'), impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, and resignation each have a trained antidote phrase ('follow the rules — they're usually right', 'not so fast, think first', 'it could happen to me', 'taking chances is foolish', 'I'm not helpless — I can make a difference').

jargon_terms.definition: Shorthand for the minimum 8 hours required between consuming alcohol and flying (91.17).
The broader preflight risk framework: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures.
Aviation Medical Examiner — the FAA-designated physician who issues pilot medical certificates.
The pilot's ongoing personal responsibility to confirm fitness to fly before every flight, medical certificate or not.

nodes.title: The Traffic Pattern
nodes.summary: Airports organize arrivals and departures into a rectangular circuit: upwind, crosswind, downwind, base, and final. Standard patterns turn LEFT, fly about 1,000 ft above the field, and make every airplane predictable.
nodes.deep_dive:
Picture a rectangle laid beside the runway, flown at pattern altitude — typically 1,000 ft AGL. Its five legs:
- Upwind (departure) leg: climbing straight out along the runway heading after takeoff.
- Crosswind: a 90° left turn, flown perpendicular to the runway while still climbing.
- Downwind: parallel to the runway, opposite the landing direction, at pattern altitude. Abeam the touchdown point, you start configuring: carb heat, power back, first flaps.
- Base: another left 90°, descending, perpendicular to the runway — the leg where you judge height and spacing.
- Final: the last turn aligns you with the runway centerline, wings level, stabilized, cleared (or self-announced) to land.

Patterns are LEFT-hand unless the airport says otherwise ('RP' on the chart, segmented circle on the field) — left turns because the pilot sits in the left seat and can see the runway throughout.

Entering at a non-towered field: the standard entry is at 45° to the downwind, at pattern altitude, aiming midfield — it gives you the longest look at existing traffic. Departing: straight out, or a 45° turn in the pattern direction after reaching pattern altitude.

Each leg has a radio call at a non-towered field, and the rhythm — announce, look, turn — is the heartbeat of pattern work. The pattern is where students live for weeks of training: every lap is a takeoff, a circuit of precise altitudes and speeds, and a landing.
nodes.advanced:
The professional-grade details. The base-to-final turn is the pattern's famous killer: overshoot the centerline, and the temptation is to steepen the bank and 'help' with inside rudder — the skidding turn that becomes a low-altitude stall/spin with no recovery room. The disciplined answer: never exceed ~30° bank in the pattern; if overshooting, go around. Stabilized-approach doctrine: by 300–500 ft AGL you are on speed (1.3 × Vso), on glidepath, configured, or you go around — go-arounds are a normal maneuver, not an apology.

Pattern-altitude taxonomy: 1,000 AGL is standard, but turbine/large aircraft fly 1,500, and the chart supplement lists exceptions. Crosswind turn: begin beyond the departure end within 300 ft of pattern altitude. AC 90-66C blesses an alternate midfield-crosswind entry (cross over the field at pattern altitude... properly: at least 500 above, descend on the far side) when arriving from the upwind side. Wake-turbulence choreography belongs to the pattern too: rotate before a preceding jet's rotation point, land beyond its touchdown point, and give 2–3 minutes behind heavies. Finally, the segmented circle beside the windsock encodes pattern direction for radio-silent aircraft: the L-shaped extensions show which side the base legs are flown on.

jargon_terms.definition: Directly off the side of — 'abeam the numbers' means beside the runway threshold, the downwind trigger point.
The published circuit height, typically 1,000 ft AGL, flown on the downwind leg.
Abandoning an approach: full power, climb, reconfigure, rejoin the pattern. A normal, trained maneuver.
The ground marking around a windsock showing traffic-pattern direction for each runway.
An approach on speed, on path, and configured by a set altitude gate — the strongest predictor of a good landing.

nodes.title: Checklists & Flows
nodes.summary: Aviation's core safety invention is embarrassingly simple: written checklists, actually used. They exist because memory fails predictably — especially under stress, interruption, and routine.
nodes.deep_dive:
In 1935 Boeing's B-17 prototype crashed on a demonstration flight because the crew — including Boeing's chief test pilot — missed one control lock. The airplane was pronounced 'too much airplane for one man to fly'. Boeing's answer was not more training; it was a piece of paper: the first formal checklist. The B-17 went on to fly 1.5 million hours safely.

A trainer's checklist set covers preflight inspection (the walk-around), before-start, start, taxi, run-up, before-takeoff, cruise, descent, before-landing, and shutdown — plus the emergency procedures section with its bold-face memory items.

Two usage styles: read-and-do (read an item, do it — used for preflight and unfamiliar procedures) and flow-then-verify (perform a practiced pattern of motions across the panel from memory, THEN read the checklist to confirm nothing was missed — how professional crews work). The verify step is the trap-catcher: a checklist you recite while looking out the window is theater, not safety.

The psychology matters more than the paper. Interruptions are the #1 checklist killer: fuel truck pulls up mid-preflight, and the seat-belt item silently vanishes. The discipline is to mark your place and restart the section — or begin the whole checklist again. Skipping 'just this once' because you have done it a thousand times is precisely how thousand-hour pilots take off with the tow bar attached.
nodes.advanced:
Deeper craft. Emergency checklists split into memory items (bold-face: engine failure's 'best glide, field, flow') executed immediately, and reference items read once the airplane is stable — knowing which is which is checkride material. The killer items concept: certain omissions are reliably fatal (controls free and correct, trim set, fuel selector, flaps, door/canopy), which is why many pilots run a short 'lineup check' mnemonic (lights-camera-action, or CIGAR-TIP variants) even after the full checklist.

Human-factors research gives this teeth: prospective memory — remembering to do a thing later — is the mind's weakest system, and it fails silently. Atul Gawande's 'Checklist Manifesto' exported the aviation lesson to surgery, cutting complications double-digit percentages. Design your own personal checklists deliberately: short (7±2 items per section), action-verb phrasing, and matched to YOUR airplane (the POH checklist is the floor, not the ceiling). Electronic checklists in glass panels track completion state — but the discipline transfers, not the burden: the box cannot know whether you actually looked at the fuel selector, only that you pressed 'checked'.

jargon_terms.definition: The pre-takeoff engine check: magnetos, carb heat, gauges — performed at the hold-short area.
Emergency steps executed immediately from memory (bold-face), before reading the full checklist.
A practiced spatial pattern of cockpit actions performed from memory, then verified against the written checklist.
The exterior preflight inspection circuit: surfaces, fuel, oil, tires, and everything hinged, latched, or leaking.

nodes.title: Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
nodes.summary: Aviation's priority hierarchy for every situation, especially emergencies: FIRST fly the airplane, THEN figure out where you are going, and only THEN talk on the radio. Order is everything.
nodes.deep_dive:
When something goes wrong, the untrained instinct is to grab the microphone. The trained response is a strict priority stack:

AVIATE. Fly the airplane. Establish and trim the correct attitude and airspeed — for an engine failure, that means best-glide speed immediately. Every accident report containing the phrase 'lost control while troubleshooting' is a violation of this line. The autopilot-era version: someone must always be flying, even when the someone is silicon being supervised.

NAVIGATE. Point the airplane somewhere useful. Engine out: pick the field and set up for it. Weather closing in: turn toward the known-good sky. Lost: climb, circle something identifiable. Only after the airplane is going where you want—

COMMUNICATE. Now the radio earns its keep: 'MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY' on the current frequency or 121.5, squawk 7700, tell them who/where/what/souls-on-board. ATC can clear airspace, call the fire trucks, and vector you — but they cannot fly the airplane, and no controller has ever kept a stalled airplane airborne by transmitting at it.

The hierarchy applies in miniature constantly: a student fumbling with a kneeboard while the nose drops is failing 'aviate'; a pilot staring at the GPS while drifting into a cloud is failing it too. Task saturation always sheds the LOWEST priority first — by design.
nodes.advanced:
The doctrine's fine print. In a real emergency, 91.3 makes the PIC's authority total: deviate from any rule to the extent required, with only a REQUESTED written report afterward (and accepting priority handling never obligates paperwork by itself — 91.3(c) asks for a report only 'upon request'). Declaring costs nothing; hesitating to say MAYDAY has cost everything. PAN-PAN covers urgency short of distress.

The engine-failure application is codified as a flow: best glide (trim for it — a 172 glides ~1.5 NM per 1,000 ft), pick the field (the one you can MAKE, not the prettiest), restart flow (fuel selector BOTH, mixture rich, carb heat, mags, primer locked), then squawk and talk. Checkride examiners watch the order like hawks. Modern crew resource management extends the trio: 'aviate' includes positive exchange of controls ('your airplane' / 'my airplane' / 'your airplane' — three-way confirmation), and workload shedding is briefed in advance: below 1,000 ft, the flying pilot flies, period. The mnemonic's origin is military flight training, and its darkest validations are cases like Eastern 401 — three crew members troubleshooting a burned-out landing-gear bulb while the L-1011 descended, unnoticed, into the Everglades.

jargon_terms.definition: The airspeed yielding maximum distance per foot of altitude lost — the first number flown after an engine failure.
The spoken distress signal, repeated three times, taking absolute priority over all other radio traffic.
Pilot In Command — the person with final authority and responsibility for the flight (14 CFR 91.3).
The overloaded state where the brain silently drops tasks — the reason priorities must be pre-decided.
